To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
OxLDL epitope distribution in xanthoma tissue is similar to macrophage distribution.

the immunohistochemical distribution and cellular localization of OxLDL and apo(a) in xanthomatas from patients with familial hpercholesterolemias are similar to each other and to the distribution of macrophages in the xanthomata.
the distribution of OxLDL epitope in xanthomats is similar to that of macrophase and is associated with macrophage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the immunohistochemical distribution and localization of lipoprotein antigens in xanthomatas.
the pathogenesis of xanthomas in familial hypercholesterol patients.
the identification of the immunohistochemical distribution and cellular localization of lipoprotein epitopes, in human xanthomata, and with the effect of treatment on these epitope distributions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the immunolocalization of Ox-LDL in xanthoma tissue is consistent with the hypothesis that Ox-LDL plays a role in the pathogenesis and/or progression of the xanthoma.
OxLDL and apo(a) are associated with macro-phages, and that LDL is present in extracellular spaces.

the immunohistochemical distribution and localization of LDL, Ox-LDL, and Lp(a) in xanthomas from patients with familial hpercholesterolemias is consistent with a role for these lipoproteins in atherosclerosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
xanthoma is the most appropriate model to study pathogenesis of atheromatosis.
the immunohistochemistry of xanthomata is consistent with the concept that the atherogenicity of LDL and Lp(a) may be mediated by the oxidation of their apolipoproteins.
OxLDL, apo(a) and LDL are present in xanthoma tissue and that OxLDL and apo(a) are associated with macro-phages.
The main takeaway from our work is that

xanthomata, which are the result of lipid deposition in the dermal tissues and subcutaneous fat, have a different distribution of lipoprotien epitopes than atherosclerotic lesions, and that the distribution of these epitopes is different than that of macrophage epitopes, suggesting that the pathogenetic mechanisms of these lesions may be different.
OxLDL, Lp(a) and LDL epitopes are associated in xanthomatas, and that these lipoproteins may play a role, along with macrophages, in the development of xanthomatous lesions.
xanthomas can be used as a model to study the pathogenesis of the atherosclerotic lesions in the vascular wall.
